- **AI & People. Same Technology. Different Human Story. AI is having a moment - and for good reason. It can make good work faster, widen access to capability, and raise the ceiling on what teams can deliver. But the impact of AI on business and the workforce is never really about the model. It’s about the humans using - and the systems we build around it. A simple way to hold the complexity is Light → Shadow → Human. Not “pro or anti” - just honest, and useful. Light: what becomes possible: Used well, AI can strip away low-value admin and create more space for judgment, creativity, care, and scientific curiosity. It can help people draft, analyse, learn, and iterate faster - and when embedded into real solid workflows, it can boost productivity. In that version of the future, we don’t just deploy tools - we build “superworkers”: people who use AI to amplify human value. Shadow: what can go wrong: The shadow isn’t “AI is bad.” It’s what happens when adoption outpaces clarity. “Disruption” lands as a human question: Am I being replaced? If fear goes unnamed, talent plans for itself….. by leaving. And without guardrails, people either avoid AI entirely or use it quietly - increasing risks like data leakage, hallucinations, bias, and accountability gaps. Worse, organisations get stuck in “pilot theatre”: lots of experiments, little trust, and no real change to the way work gets done. Human: the outcome depends on our choices: This is where leadership matters. The practical moves are not abstract: Plan by tasks, not job titles. Automate tasks; elevate roles. Ask: what human value do we want more of? Build trust on purpose. Don’t promise “AI won’t change jobs.” Promise: your job is safe to evolve here - then prove it with clear boundaries, involvement in workflow design, and visible pathways to reskill. Equip everyone. Make training inclusive: basics for all, team support, and a leader track. Remember: mentoring beats more training. Build safe courage. Create a “safe to try” bundle: approved tools, data rules, templates, red flags, escalation paths, and a learning community. And one final reminder: even when AI isn’t mandated, it can change habits. Harvard Business Review shared in-progress research suggesting AI often doesn’t reduce work - it can intensify it, as people do more simply because it feels possible. That’s another reason the “Human” piece matters: we have to design sustainable ways of working, not just faster ones. Same technology. Same data. Different human story. The story we get is the one we choose to build. ...more**

- **Yesterday at Digital Pharma Advances conference, I had the privilege of co-chairing the afternoon session with Alan How (Digital Lead, Bayer) and leading a panel on AI, Regulation & Compliance. What stood out most wasn’t a single tool or platform - it was how fundamentally AI is reshaping where authority, trust, and relevance sit in pharma. AI has become the red thread running through everything we do: powerful, yes but deeply disruptive. One idea resonated strongly: AI creates ripples, not straight lines. No single function can manage those ripples alone. It truly takes a village - multiple functions working together early and often. One important shift we kept coming back to: patients now have access to detailed medical knowledge at unprecedented depth through AI-generated answers. Information that was once gated is now immediately available. This reality forces pharma to re-earn relevance, not rely on controlled access to information. In an AI-rich world: Information is abundant. Trust is not And trust, as we discussed repeatedly, compounds over time. We also talked about something more uncomfortable: AI often reverts to the mean. Its answers can be statistically sound yet fundamentally average. That’s where humans still matter most. Humans bring: Intuition, empat, judgement - the gut feel that context demands. AI is an extraordinary tool - but it works best paired with human inventiveness and compassion, not used as a replacement. Several other themes stayed with me: From talking to responding: moving from brands deciding message and timing to patients and HCPs deciding the question and the moment. Curiosity is now the strongest engagement signal. Discoverability matters: if people ask AI first and don’t find credible pharma content, someone else answers for us. People still matter more than platforms: many organisations are juggling multiple AI tools. The real question isn’t what tools we have, but how users know what to use, when. Human mentoring consistently beats more training. We also acknowledged the reality of operating in motion: Guardrails are constantly evolving. Portfolio thinking matters more than isolated pilots. AI literacy is foundational. ROI is hard to pin down, so rapid prototyping and AI Centres of Excellence should act as feasibility and value engines, not just governance bodies. The future isn’t about more noise. It’s about earning trust - deliberately, collaboratively, and over time. Huge thanks to GIC – Global Insights Conferences for the invitation to speak and co-chair. #DigitalPharmaAdvances ...more**

- **The Best Fuel at Work? Feeling Valued. Some of us have had a chance to relax, switch off, and leave work alone for a few days. So before it gets busy again……..remember this: Sometimes work gets noisy. Ten people. Ten opinions. Two directions. And a whole lot of “urgent” flying around. In those moments, I’ve learned to do two things at the same time: • Listen properly (because you can always learn something) • Stick to your guns (because experience counts for a reason) Not in an ego way. Not in a “my way or the highway” way. More like: “This is what I’m seeing, this is why I’m concerned, and this is what I think will actually work.” And when you keep saying it calmly, consistently, and with evidence… something shifts. You get heard. The idea lands. What you’ve been pushing for gets adopted. And honestly? That’s when any residual lethargy just melts away. Because feeling valued isn’t a fluffy extra. It’s fuel. It’s the best tonic there is for getting your drive back. The goal isn’t to “win” the argument. It’s to stay true to what you believe, invite challenge, and then build something together that everyone can own. That’s the sweet spot. ...more**

- **If We Want Transformation, Where’s the Belief? We talk a lot about transformation. Digital. Cultural. AI. All of it. But here’s the questions I keep coming back to: Where is the belief system behind it? How does it manifest in the real world? Where’s the physical, visible commitment from leadership? Because here’s the uncomfortable truth: Many staff go along with transformation out of fear. Fear of being left behind. Of being labelled resistant. Of losing their jobs. But on the flip side? Execs often hold back for the exact same reason. Fear. Not of being left behind - but of taking a risk that might not land. Of being the one who backed the “wrong” move. That’s the paradox. And that’s the gap a good transformation leader has to bridge. We have to create a belief system that everyone can connect with. Not just a vision slide or a buzzword-filled roadmap. But something real. Tangible. A future people can see themselves in - and trust. If your org has tried and failed before (or done it half-baked)? That belief is even harder to build. Because people remember. They say: “What’s the point? It’ll just fizzle out like last time.” And they’re not wrong - unless something is different this time. Unless the belief is truly shared. From the top. From the middle. From the people who’ll actually make it happen. That means leaders, at all levels, can’t play political games behind the scenes. You can’t have one exec going all in while another quietly ignores progress. Transformation fails in dissonance. It thrives in alignment. And that alignment only happens when the belief system is clear, shared, and lived - not just written down. #TransformationLeadership #DigitalChange #LeadershipMatters #OrganisationalChange #CulturalShift #BeliefDrivesChange ...more**

- **Throughout my career across Europe and the US, I've sat through countless discussions about "breaking down silos", "working cross-functionally" and "fostering collaboration". Most organisations recognise the problem. Many invest heavily in solving it. Yet the same barriers persist. Over time, I've come to believe that's because we often focus on the wrong walls. We look at structures, reporting lines and processes. Yes, those things matter, but some of the most significant barriers are less visible. They're the assumptions we make about where expertise sits. The tendency to stay within our own function because it's familiar. Or the belief that our team, our market or our discipline has the best view of the problem… Since joining Kyowa Kirin International plc. , I've been introduced to a concept that speaks directly to this challenge: Kabegoe. In Japanese, it means "leaping over walls". At Kyowa Kirin, Kabegoe is an active leadership framework of 11 principles anchored by our four core values: Commitment to Life, Integrity, Innovation, and Teamwork (Wa). What resonates with me is that Kabegoe isn't really about organisational design. It's about mindset. It's a reminder that the most valuable insight may come from someone with a completely different perspective. That solving a complex problem often starts with being curious enough to look beyond your own expertise. And that progress accelerates when people are willing to cross boundaries rather than defend them. To serve patients with innovative medicines, this matters more than ever. The challenges we face span science, regulation, healthcare systems, technology and patient care. No single function or leadership team can fully understand every dimension. The breakthroughs that matter most often happen when different perspectives come together around a shared goal. Practically, this means being willing to ask for input before you have the answer. To invite challenge rather than consensus. To acknowledge that experience, while valuable, can sometimes become a wall in itself. I've certainly had to learn that lesson more than once throughout my career. Because in the end, innovation is rarely about a single brilliant idea. More often, it's about connecting insights that already exist across an organisation – and creating an environment where people feel empowered to bring them together.**
